Stated Claim / Post Context:
Requiem for the American Dream: A nation in search of its past, with fragile hopes for its future

There are a lot of ghosts here, but they’re the kinds of hauntings that we live with, day by day. They’re the ghosts who remind us the past really is prologue. But the future is unwritten.

Trending:

The first thing you notice is the eyes, the uncertainty, the exhaustion.

The next thing you notice is the history, the way every past holds layers.

Nothing is new, but everything looks unsettled.

Earlier this year, with the country’s 250th anniversary in mind, Tribune photojournalist E. Jason Wambsgans set out to take the collective temperature. He roamed every corner of Illinois and returned with a portrait of a state — and a nation — at a crossroads. Poignant images of people and places across Illinois that illustrate a vibe, a feeling, that up-in-the-air quality not so different from what national polls are reporting.

The mood of the United States of America before the midterm elections next month is sour, grim, uneasy, dyspeptic, distrustful, anxious, unsettled. Take your pick. A solid year of polling is saying, pretty consistently, that you and everyone you know, for the most part, are uncertain about this country. In fact, you are so doubtful and tentative about the future, the only thing you agree on, generally, is being a United States in name only.

A majority of us believe the best years of the country “are behind us” (Pew Research). A majority feel the American Dream was once achievable decades ago but no longer is (AP-NORC). A majority say the state of the union is not strong (NPR/PBS News/Marist), and, according to another national survey (North Carolina’s Elon University), more than two thirds of Americans believe the signers of the Declaration of Independence would be disappointed by how their descendants are managing democracy 250 years later.

Still, as ugly as it sounds, glimmers of light persist, here and there, in these same polls: A majority of us feel proud to be American, and most hold a sliver of hope for the future.

Sounds like a paradox.

Except, polling doesn’t show you individuals and it doesn’t tell their stories and it can’t explain circumstances. By design, a poll is a statistical snapshot of a feeling. It doesn’t account for decades of local history, or how a landscape itself can inform feelings. All of that, though, is glimpsed in these photos, a fragility seated alongside a resilience. There are a lot of ghosts here, but they’re the kinds of hauntings that we live with, day by day.

They’re the ghosts who remind us the past really is prologue. But the future is unwritten.

It was an unconventional way to reach people in 2026. “Certainly super old school,” Maurice West said. Like, centuries old. West represents the 67th District in the Illinois House (which includes Rockford and some surrounding communities), and he agreed last summer to read the Declaration of Independence as part of the ongoing Illinois 250 initiative. He read beneath a soaring white oak on the grounds of Tinker Swiss Cottage Museum and Gardens. Only a smattering of people turned out, the majority of them older.

Before he read, he told the assembled that yes, the world feels like chaos, but please remember what unites them. As he read, he thought about his life as a Black man; he thought of how the word “patriotic” often sounds divisive now; he thought about the phrase “the pursuit of happiness” and how “your pursuit of happiness may not look like mine, yet still you have the right. And we seem to be walking away from that — when your pursuit doesn’t look like mine, you’re going to hell, you’re an enemy of the country.”

All of that ran through his head. When he looked up, he recognized a few people. He knew their politics were not his. “Some people wore red, white and blue. Nine times out of ten, that’s Trump Country these days. Nine times out of ten, as a Black man, I know how you feel. But I felt welcome there. Really I had no idea of anyone’s ideology. That became the best part.” A month later, West announced he’s running for mayor of Rockford.

A 15-minute drive from Shawneetown is Equality, Illinois. It was founded on salt-mining wealth. The Crenshaw House was a totem of this fortune, constructed by a businessman named James Crenshaw. He was so rich that his taxes amounted to 15 percent of the state’s entire revenue.

Though Illinois became a free state in 1818, he also was known for still owning slaves, being part of a small group of Illinois residents granted an exemption because their slaves worked federally owned salt mines.

Even more notoriously, Crenshaw — who walked with a mangled leg after one of his slaves attacked him with an axe — used this home as a jail for Black residents he kidnapped and sold to slave states, including Kentucky and Texas. It was known as “The Reverse Underground Railroad,” and Crenshaw, who was arrested for kidnapping but acquitted, eventually built actual railroads and later served as the president of the Bank of Illinois.

The Kaskaskia Bell was cast in 1741, gifted to the village of Kaskaskia by King Louis XV. It was the first capitol of the new Illinois Territory, and for decades, reliant on labor provided by slave plantations operated by French Jesuits.

Nevertheless, during the Revolutionary War, after Kaskaskia was reclaimed from British forces, it was rung in the name of liberty. A century on, shifting floodwaters along the Mississippi River reduced Kaskaskia to an island.

Today, its population is 21, the third-smallest in the state. The bell still hangs here, but it’s accessible only from Missouri, and according to the State Historic Preservation Office, there are no tours available and there are “no places to sit.”

Mikaela Martin is 24, but when she plays a Civil War soldier, she looks 144. That thousand-yard stare is no joke. Most days she’s a counselor with a mental health service in Hazel Crest. But about 10 times a year, she’s a female soldier, a private with the 100th Illinois Infantry Company K. “I’ve been barred from some groups because of who I am,” she said, “because they think only a man can play this role. The majority of (reenactors) are supportive, but misogyny is real, it happens — from the public, too. One time a guy watching us yelled, ‘Hey, that’s a woman!’ Well, yeah, and that’s history, too.”

Historians figure somewhere as many as 1,000 Civil War soldiers, across both sides of the conflict, were women enlisted as men, so they could fight. The best known case in Illinois was Belvidere resident Albert Cashier, born in Ireland as Jennie Hodgers. Cashier fought for three years, then returned to Illinois and lived as a man until dying in 1915.

“I’m doing it to represent this small percentage of women,” Martin said. “It’s important to me to educate people about women’s roles beyond the usual duties they had in the war. We don’t really know how many did this because they wouldn’t go to doctors when they were wounded. They would dig bullets out of themselves, or ignore injuries until they were discovered or dead. So yes, I am haunted in this role. I’m general infantry and I believe in the cause against slavery. I’ve fought and probably been shot a few times.

“It leads me to think a lot about political unrest now, and the unrest of 150 years ago. They wondered if the United States could stay together, when brother fought brother and family fought family. That resonates with me, and this sounds weird to say, but it comforts me. It tells me good can conquer evil, and eventually even this too shall pass.”

Jim Barker’s small parcel of farm in McLeansboro, northeast of Shawnee National Forest, is something of a local attraction, a regular gawk for motorists. Color photos of the place could be an AI prompt for Eden, a towering kaleidoscopic sea of reds and lilacs and yellows, sweet Black-eyed Susans, golden rod, asters, rattlesnake masters. Part of this land was original Illinois prairie, which Barker has spent years trying to restore.

The showstoppers are the long spikes of purple and pink wildflowers, a native Illinois plant named blazing stars. Barker began with a handful in 2009. He first noticed them alongside Route 142, near the village of Belle Rive. They were growing because the state, in an attempt to trim its budget, cut back on how often it mowed grass beside its highways. “They had taken so long to mow those blazing stars had grown and bloomed, and I wanted some.” He climbed out of his car and collected a handful of the seeds.

Later he confessed to a friend who works for the state. She told him harvesting seeds on a highway is illegal. He confessed to a state trooper, who told him not to worry. Nobody’s ever complained. He has 150 blazing stars today. Garden clubs visit. He even registered for the Conservation Reserve Program, a federal initiative that pays farmers to stop planting crops in certain areas to encourage a revival of wildlife and pollinators.

The Shawneetown Bank, east of Carbondale, sits along the banks of the Ohio River, near what was once a prosperous salt mine. It was built high enough to ensure it would never be flooded. It was the first bank in Illinois. It helped finance the capital in Springfield, though, according to legend, representatives of the nascent town of Chicago visited, asking for a loan to expand.

To sweeten the deal, a branch of the bank was proposed in Chicago. Shawneetown turned down both ideas. In hindsight, this might have been a good thing: Soon there were disastrous bank runs, southern disinvestment during the Civil War and, finally, in 1937, unprecedented 20-foot high flood waters. The buildings have been unused since 1942.

It’s a common misconception that Sauganash, in northwest Chicago, is an official neighborhood, when it actually is a district within the official neighborhood of Forest Glen. Its name is Potawatomi for “English-speaking,” and was coined by Billy Caldwell, the half Irish-half Mohawk son of a British officer. Caldwell helped negotiate the treaty that stripped resident Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa tribes of this land. A century later, a real estate firm with plans to build on a quiet spot about 10 miles from downtown Chicago, placed a marker by a large elm tree, commemorating where the treaty was signed. According to the Sauganash Community Association, since the treaty was signed at Fort Dearborn, the plaque (still there) was a prop, to lend the development a good story.

If you’ve ever heard of Farmer City, which is midway between Champaign and Bloomington, it’s either because, in the late 1800s, the downtown was destroyed twice by fire in 15 years, or because the local council passed a resolution in 2018 that declared Farmer City to be a “Second Amendment sanctuary city.” Any gun legislation they consider excessive will not be enforced here. It’s not a big place, maybe 1,800 people, pretty quiet, a quintessential everyone-knows-everyone’s-business sort of place.

Danielle Bettinger was watching fireworks in a backyard. She went to pharmacy school in Chicago. She prefers Farmer City. She never worries if her three sons are going to get hurt here, she said. She prefers the safety of a small town. These fireworks, for instance, were paid for by neighbors, who pooled cash together. “What I noticed was my kids loved the idea of fireworks but not so much the explosions and the loud sounds.”

Her middle son is obsessed with wearing the U.S. flag on his shirts. The older one opts for military camouflage. They all live in a home with Bettinger’s mother and sister. She said the country seems like it’s doing fine, but it’s too expensive. She figures she spends upwards of $200 a week on groceries, just for her and the kids. “The problem is, inflation is not something that people can really control. We can’t do a thing about it.”

Ruth Julian stood sentinel on a corner of Wheaton, by the library. She didn’t have a sign when she arrived, but others, the teenagers who organized the protest, had cardboard and markers. On one side, Julian wrote “REJECT AI!” On the other, “SAY NO TO DATA CENTERS!” There were honks of agreement, and every so often a middle finger. Not that protesting is ever tidy: She was out there on a national day of resistance to data centers that had been proposed initially by Humans First, a grassroots anti-AI group founded by Trump supporters. An Indiana native, she was not always a willing protestor. Then, around 2016, “I found my voice — you see people being harmed, you see things happening in this country that are just not right, and once it’s seen, you don’t unsee it.”

She was once a missionary; then she walked dogs for a while; and now she’s a therapist, focused on the Japanese tradition of shiatsu bodywork. She’s 63. She came to this corner because of a No Kings protest. “My friend and I went and it was great and then … everyone went home. I was like, what is this? Are we treating this like just another day in the park? We decided to hand out flyers and find a group who would stay involved regularly. A few people reached out, and then this 16-year-old also joined up.”

And so now, in the western suburbs, there’s a small group text of about 10 people, an intergenerational one, elderly protestors, college students, high school students. “Do I ever feel lonely doing this? I feel in solidarity. Will any of it, standing there with a sign, make a difference? I don’t know. You raise awareness anyway because if you’re not aware, you can’t do anything. Young people give me hope. Man, you gotta have hope.”

You can find the sign in Amboy, near Dixon. Duct tape was invented here, and the department store chain Carson Pirie Scott opened its first store here in 1855, before turning to Chicago. For a time, Amboy was promising enough that it was expected to become the seat of Lee County. But Dixon had more potential.

Only 2,278 people live there today. And that includes Brad Anderson, who was born with a disease that affects his spine. When he was 26, he was moving railroad ties at work and a bunch of his muscles started working overtime to do the job a spine normally would. Eventually, his back gave out. He’s 61 now and been on disability for 35 years: “It’s a piss-poor way to live. I was active, and there’s nothing worse than being bored.”

In 2015, after Donald Trump announced his first presidential run, Anderson noticed there were no signs of support nearby. “So my dad and I decided to make our own.” They painted “Trump” in red, “Evil” in blue, “Slayer” in red, coded to the political parties. It’s a rare day when a passing car doesn’t honk in support or a driver flash him a thumbs-up. “People around here feel positive on Trump. Things are tough right now but it’s a temporary feeling. Life goes on, better times are ahead. I think this is all run by God, really. People vote for (Trump) thinking of their kids and family bloodlines. They know he’s about making the world safe. You have to have hope, otherwise, why vote?”

Judge LaShondra A. Hunt couldn’t remember the last time she administered a citizenship oath. She couldn’t recall the last time she led a naturalization ceremony at Dirksen federal courthouse in the Loop, home of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. Before her this day were 88 people from 34 countries. When she joined the district court three years ago, naturalization ceremonies were routine; she did them all the time. Dirksen alone swore in 29,000 new citizens a year. Now it’s closer to 5,000.

Typically she reads off a script. She didn’t this time.

She decided to make two points: The first is to recognize that becoming a citizen is very difficult; there’s the process, the money, the forms, the waiting. “I made sure to say it’s emotionally taxing, too, because there are people left behind, there are cultures left behind. And yet, they have come this far.”

The other point she made is that this is a responsibility — there are people who have not made it this far who continue to wait. “I like to tell them, ‘Yes, now you have access to freedoms, liberties, but you also have a responsibility to vote, serve on a jury, teach your children what being a citizen means.’”

She didn’t avoid the anxiety of the moment. Before she finished, she said it’s a difficult moment for their new country, still they have faced difficult times before, so the question before them is, how do we push past this and remember what it means to be American?

Usually at this point, she scans their faces, and she can’t help notice the tears.

Four years ago the local Boy Scout chapter in of St. Joseph Township decided to start an annual Fourth of July parade. In deference to any older parades nearby — courteousness being one of the 12 core values of the Boy Scouts — they only march July 3. At the front of the line is always Jared Durst, because, as his father James Durst explained, Jared has to be in front, always. That’s how he is. He’s 13 and small for his age, but proud. He’s named for a great-grand-uncle whom James never met, but he was struck by his story: The first Jared Durst attended University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign a century ago and studied truck farming, or growing your own produce and selling it out of your own truck, direct to locals. (Think farmers markets, farm-to-table.)

He made it through a year of school before being pulled into World War I. He was stationed at Camp Grant in Rockford. While in training, Jared caught Spanish flu and died. Of the camp’s 4,000 soldiers, more than a quarter succumbed to influenza, never leaving Rockford. (The camp closed in 1946, and the land became Rockford’s airport.)

The day Jared 2026 marched, the scouts complained it was hot. James told them: “This would be a cold day in Vietnam! You people can put up with 30 minutes of heat.”

With 3,800 residents, St. Joseph is just west of Champaign. James said they don’t have the problems of other suburbs, folks are content. But: “We’re tired, we’re tired of politics, and you do hear, ‘Will I still have a job tomorrow?’”

Cameron Crowley always looks like this after work. Every single day, he laughs. He works underground, drives a mining car for a coal facility in southern Illinois. Miners cut coal and load it into his car, he deposits it onto a conveyor belt. He does this from 3 in the afternoon until about 2 in the morning. A century ago, there were at least 1,350 mines in Illinois; today there are fewer than 20. Crowley is 24. He figures he’ll be doing this until he’s 63. “At least, I hope. They tell us there’s at least 20 years left in this mine.”

He once worked on a pipeline in Arkansas. This is better. “My favorite job ever, and also the hardest I’ve ever worked.” Seventy-hour weeks are routine. Crowley dropped out of school in 10th grade, assuming he’d be doing manual labor all his life, anyway. He speaks in a heavy, tired drawl. He sounds decades older than he is. No, he doesn’t know how his window got cracked. But until recently, he couldn’t afford to get it fixed.

He lives in an unincorporated rural area called Crab Orchard. “This job, I might make more than a lot of people my age. But gas prices are going up, grocery prices going up. Buying a house, getting a new vehicle — you definitely can’t do that.” He drives a 1995 Chevy pickup with more than 200,000 miles on it. There used to be a union in the mine, but no longer. He doesn’t believe the government cares. Like the people he works with, he blames Illinois’ Democratic leadership for the problems, the prices. “Considering how much this part of the state is forgotten, cost of living here is more than you’d think.”

Despite impressions, neither Garrett Kasput nor Colin Eason have much interest in joining the military. Both are 18, both graduated high school in the spring and both come from families with decades of veterans.

“But no, I’m good, thanks,” Eason said. “Considering how everything is looking now in Iran.”

Instead, they dressed as War-on-Terror era soldiers during Lockport Military History Weekend in the fall. Kasput started first. Several years ago at the event, he bought a camouflaged coat, an artifact of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, then acquired more, until he had a full suit. Eason decided to match Kasput, partly using gear gifted to him by his father, who served in the 1990s.

Lockport Military History Weekend began a few decades ago primarily as a Civil War reenactment weekend, then broadened into World War I and World War II and Vietnam War reenactments. War-on-Terror is niche here. Kasput and Eason tend to be outliers.

“A lot of people in (military) cosplay show off their interest,” Kasput said. “I’m not so outward, and the more I learn about controversial details (of the War on Terror), since the current administration isn’t too popular, considering general unrest in the Middle East, the more I’m more aware of the history, it wouldn’t be appropriate to openly advertise this.”

In lieu of the military, Eason wants “a trade with a pension, though nobody offers pensions now.” Kasput is going into software development, though absolutely not AI.

The white-haired man at the end of the row is Robert Wapahi-mami. He is carrying what he always carries at a powwow, a POW/MIA flag. This was last summer in Pilsen. The Grand Entry, the formal opening, begins with a color guard, U.S. and Canadian flags, and at the head of the procession, an Eagle Staff coated in feathers. “Its place is intentional,” said Jay Young, executive director of the American Indian Center in Albany Park. “It speaks to Native people, and our sovereignty, and that our communities are still here.” Veterans, however, receive a special place, representing not only those who served in the U.S. military, but those who protected tribes long before this nation existed.

Wapahi-mami, 81, served more than two years in Vietnam. He felt a contradiction in that service back then, and he still feels it now: “Basically, I was fighting on the side of those who once hunted me.” He grew up on the Santee Sioux reservation in Nebraska, where much of the community had settled after being forced out of Minnesota in the 1860s. A century later, Wapahi-mami, Santee descendant, was still being relocated, driven to Chicago with other Santee, as part of a Bureau of Indian Affairs program: “We were dropped off downtown and handed a month’s rent and just told to make the best of it.”

While he held that flag, he thought of the soldiers he served with who never had a chance to finish their lives. “But to be honest, I also try not to think a whole lot about it. My first thought tends to be anger. Yes, everyone gets their time at the top of the social scale, but I’ve never really been comfortable with being a minority in my own home.”

The day before was 103 degrees. A day later, it was a nice Sunday afternoon, small breeze even. Ron Malisia was grateful. Some years, when the town of Panama, which sits midway between St. Louis and Springfield, pop. 337, lines up for its annual Mulligan Stew dinner, the sun is brutal. Worse, everyone is lugging their own pots, to stock up, knowing Mulligan Stew won’t be back for another year, always on Labor Day weekend.

Certainly it’s one of the least-known, and most specific, of Midwestern culinary traditions. In 1946, John Malisia, Ron’s father, returned from World War II, having spent much of his time as a mechanic, working on Jeeps. “It was said he worked on Patton’s Jeep, though we never confirmed that — my father wouldn’t talk about the war much.” He returned to a Panama that was losing mining jobs, and looking poorer, and hungrier. “So he and some farmers decided to bring in chickens who weren’t producing eggs, beef, turtles, carrots, beans, onions, garlic, potatoes, cabbage — and throw it all into 35-gallon kettles.” They slow-cooked it and named it Mulligan Stew, inviting the town to a big free meal. For decades, it was all free. You got a bowl, a spoon and oyster crackers.

Now it’s $5 a ladle.

But the tradition never died, and a community food line is now a neighborly celebration. The VFW took over the job years ago, though little else changed. “Nothing was ever particularly rich around here,” Malisia said. They start gathering food Thursday, begin cooking Saturday night, then serve Sunday, at high noon. “Hobo stew,” some call it now.

And what’s it taste like?

“Well, not chicken.”

Once a month, a shipment of food arrives at a mobile pantry in New Douglas. It comes from St. Louis, 40 miles away. It’s not always the freshest, said Marina Brenham, who started volunteering at the pantry 11 years ago. But some take it, anyway. Since she began handing out food at the pantry — often driving to people who can’t make it to her truck — she’s seen demand go way, way up. Entire families come, hoping for anything. Sometimes they’re her neighbors. Usually they come from struggling rural communities.

Brenham, 68, lives in nearby Sorento, where it takes at least half an hour for an ambulance to reach your house. Four years ago, she had a kidney transplant. She wants to do more but it slowed her down. Lately, she’s more worried about citizenship. She grew up in Germany, she has lived in this country for 40 years; she has her citizenship. “I came with a Green Card, I volunteered for decades, I supported the troops, and yet, I am scared, I am scared — I never thought things would get this bad.”

Not every member of the South Shore Drill Team wants to be seen. Some prefer the anonymity of dozens of teammates surrounding them, everyone twirling a wood rifle in a matching uniform, no one member the focus of cameras or crowds. Javoni Luckett, 12, is different. At the annual Bud Billiken Parade in August, he stared down cameras with a natural poise, charisma evident. “We train them to do it, actually,” said Melvin Coleman, his instructor. “We teach them to stay calm, to be aware people are looking at them.”

The South Shore Drill Team was founded in 1980 by school teacher Arthur Robertson (who is still involved). He wanted a military-precision color guard. He got four recruits. Forty-six years later, he has 80, the youngest being 7, the oldest 22. They train five days a week, and perform at about 75 events a year. They are immortalized in the parade scene in “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off,” and in 2013 alone, they started the year at the inauguration of Barack Obama and ended at the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Bud Billiken marks the peak of their calendar, the oldest Black parade in the nation, winding through Bronzeville into Washington Park, coming up on its 100th year in 2029. Muhammad Ali marched here, Duke Ellington, Harry S. Truman, Billie Holiday. And now Javoni Luckett, whose family marched with the drill team for decades before him. “Next year Javoni might be with our older kids,” Coleman said. “He’s climbing the ladder here, he’s getting really skilled. He’s a fast learner, and a good kid — so he’s right in the front.”

Khyira Holloway and Dhashon Dyson, sister and brother, walked slowly out of Lake Michigan in August with the flush of renewal, ready to face the next part of their lives. Here at 63rd Street Beach, they agreed to get baptized together, just after dawn. Dyson, 25, plays professional basketball overseas; he was home between seasons. He decided to get baptized to mark a turning point, being on his own, making his own decisions, growing closer to God: “There was nothing forced about it,” he said. Holloway, 28, is a beautician, specializing in eyelashes; she’s doing well lately, she said. She was baptized to show a trust in faith: “It’s like I’m turning away from my old life, surrendering myself.”

But not long ago, “my brother and I, we were going through a lot together. Financially, everything had fallen out. My family, my mother, everyone — financially struggling. Just living was hard. My dad made sure the household went on. And I was in a place where I lost everything. I was around people I had no business being around. I lost my house, my car, my business. I felt like everyone was against me. I went into solitude for like three years. I was at my lowest. My brother was playing overseas, so I was by myself a lot.” Dyson had never been out of the country, and now he was meeting coaches who had never spoken to a Black person: “Life was much slower, but the food was healthier.”

After he returned to Chicago, his family decided to repair their lives and attend church together, like they did decades ago, living near Washington Park. He started to alternate jobs, playing professional basketball overseas while teaching part time in Chicago Public Schools. Holloway, meanwhile, fell back in love with beauty. Clients returned. She credits God, but said the path that led to their baptism, that was scary. “You don’t know what’s next, you put faith in a spiritual being you can’t see, but you know is real.”
